memory: I've learned to be more mindful of my health as I've gotten older. It's amazing how much of a difference small lifestyle changes can make. And living in Kansas with its unpredictable weather means I have to be flexible with my routine. Some days I can get outside and enjoy a long walk, but other times I'm stuck inside due to the cold winters or severe storms. Despite the challenges, I try to stay active, eat well, and manage my stress levels. It's all about finding that balance. I've made significant changes to my diet since being diagnosed with Type 2 Diabetes. I've learned to be mindful of my carb intake and have replaced pasta and bread with healthier options like whole grains, lean proteins, and plenty of vegetables. It was tough at first, but now it's just second nature. My go-to breakfast is Greek yogurt with nuts and berries or eggs with avocado. For lunch, I keep it simple with grilled chicken and a salad. And for dinner, I love making soups, especially during the winter. There's nothing better than a warm bowl of homemade vegetable soup on a freezing day!One of the biggest things I’ve noticed is how my metabolism has slowed down. I used to be able to eat whatever I wanted, but now if I’m not careful, the weight creeps up on me. I focus on eating more protein, healthy fats, and fiber to keep my digestion in check. Processed foods make me feel sluggish, so I try to cook most of my meals at home. One of my favorite go-to meals is grilled salmon with roasted vegetables—it’s simple, delicious, and packed with nutrients that help with inflammation.Exercise has also changed for me. I used to think workouts had to be intense to be effective, but I’ve learned that consistency is more important. I walk every day, rain or shine, even if it’s just around my neighborhood. Strength training is something I’ve started doing more of, too. My doctor told me that muscle loss accelerates as you get older, and maintaining strength is key to preventing injuries. I do light weights and resistance bands a few times a week—nothing too crazy, but it helps a lot with my balance and joint health.Sleep has become another priority. I used to be fine on five or six hours of sleep, but now if I don't get a solid seven or eight, I feel it the next day. I've had to work on my sleep hygiene—no screens an hour before bed, a cool and dark room, and sticking to a consistent schedule. I also started taking magnesium supplements, and they've really helped with relaxation. It's funny how something as simple as getting enough sleep can make such a huge difference in how I feel.Oh! And my skin. I never used to worry about it, but now I’m all about hydration and sunscreen. I wear SPF every day, even in the winter, because sun damage adds up over the years. I also drink a ton of water, which helps keep my skin from feeling dry, especially during Kansas winters. I’ve started using a retinol cream at night, too—apparently, it’s great for keeping skin healthy as you age. Not that I’m trying to look 30 again, but I do want to keep my skin looking and feeling good!One thing I didn't expect about aging is how important social connections are. It's so easy to get caught up in work, family, and responsibilities, but having a good support system really helps with mental well-being. I make it a point to have coffee with friends at least once a week, and I joined a book club last year. It's been such a great way to stay engaged and meet new people. I truly believe staying socially active keeps you young!Let’s talk about memory. I wouldn’t say I’m forgetful, but I definitely have more ‘where did I put my keys?’ moments than I used to. I try to keep my brain sharp by doing puzzles, reading, and even learning new skills. I started taking an online class on art history just for fun, and it’s been such a great mental exercise. They say lifelong learning helps prevent cognitive decline, so I figure it’s worth a shot!One of the challenges I’ve faced is managing chronic pain. My osteoarthritis acts up more in the colder months, and some days, my joints feel stiff no matter what I do. I’ve found that warm baths with Epsom salts help, and I also swear by using a heating pad in the mornings. My doctor recommended I try tai chi or gentle stretching, so I’ve been looking into that as well. I’m learning that aging isn’t about avoiding discomfort altogether—it’s about finding ways to manage it so I can keep doing what I love.Overall, I’m embracing aging. Sure, there are challenges, but there’s also so much wisdom that comes with experience. I’ve learned to listen to my body, take care of myself, and appreciate the little things more. If I could give advice to my younger self, I’d say: don’t stress about the small stuff, take care of your health early, and enjoy every stage of life. Getting older isn’t something to fear—it’s just another chapter!I've been keeping track of my medical test reports over the years, and it's interesting to see how things have changed. I always try to stay on top of my health by getting regular check-ups, especially with my history of diabetes and hypertension. My latest bloodwork had some ups and downs, but nothing too alarming. Living in Kansas, where the seasons affect everything from my energy levels to my joint pain, I've learned to keep a close eye on my numbers so I can adjust my lifestyle as needed.Let me break it down for you. My most recent fasting blood glucose test came back at 135 mg/dL, which is a bit higher than I'd like—it should ideally be under 100 mg/dL. My A1C was 6.9%, which is just above the target range of 6.5%, meaning I need to be more careful with my carb intake. My doctor suggested adding more fiber to my diet and making sure I get some light exercise after meals. I've also been checking my blood sugar at home, and my morning readings tend to hover around 125-130 mg/dL.My cholesterol numbers were a mixed bag. My total cholesterol was 195 mg/dL, which is okay, but my LDL(bad cholesterol) was 130 mg/dL—higher than the recommended under 100 mg/dL. On the bright side, my HDL(good cholesterol) was 58 mg/dL, which is in a good range. My triglycerides were 140 mg/dL, which is slightly elevated but not too concerning. My doctor advised me to increase my intake of healthy fats like avocados and nuts and to cut back on saturated fats.Blood pressure has always been something I need to monitor. At my last check-up, my reading was 138/85 mmHg, which is on the high side. My doctor wants me to aim for below 130/80 mmHg to keep my risk of heart issues lower. I've been keeping track of it at home, and my readings fluctuate between 135-140 systolic and 80-90 diastolic, depending on my stress levels and salt intake. I'm trying to cut back on sodium and drink more water, which seems to help.One test that surprised me was my vitamin D levels. I thought I was getting enough sunlight, but my levels came back at 22 ng/mL, which is considered deficient. The normal range is 30-50 ng/mL, so my doctor put me on a vitamin D supplement. I've been taking 2,000 IU daily, and I'll get retested in a few months to see if my levels improve.Oh! And my thyroid numbers were stable this time, which was a relief. My TSH was 2.1 mIU/L, which is right in the normal range(0.5-4.5 mIU/L). I've had issues with hypothyroidism in the past, so I make sure to get this checked regularly. My T4 levels were also good at 1.2 ng/dL, meaning my current dosage of levothyroxine is working well.My bone density scan showed a slight decline. My T-score for my spine was -1.8, which is considered osteopenia(the stage before osteoporosis). My hip T-score was -1.5, which is also in the borderline range. My doctor advised me to keep up with strength training and calcium intake to prevent further bone loss. I've started adding more dairy and leafy greens to my diet, plus I take a calcium supplement with vitamin K2 to help with absorption.Liver and kidney function tests were mostly fine, but my ALT levels were a little elevated at 42 U/L(normal is under 35 U/L). My doctor thinks it might be related to some recent medication adjustments, so we're going to keep an eye on it. My creatinine levels were at 0.9 mg/dL, which is well within the normal range(0.6-1.2 mg/dL), so no concerns with kidney function.One thing I was really curious about was my inflammatory markers. My C-reactive protein(CRP) was at 3.2 mg/L, which is slightly elevated(ideal is under 3.0 mg/L), indicating some mild inflammation—probably related to my osteoarthritis. My ESR(erythrocyte sedimentation rate) was 18 mm/hr, which is within the normal range(0-20 mm/hr), so at least there's no major inflammation going on.Overall, I'm feeling good about my latest test results, but there are definitely things I need to work on—mainly keeping my blood sugar in check and getting my vitamin D levels up. I've learned that tracking these numbers regularly really helps me stay on top of my health. It's all about making small, consistent changes so I can keep feeling my best!
